Q: How do you evaluate semantic boundaries without confusing chunk size with retrieval quality?
A:
Chunking decides which evidence remains together and which context must be recovered later. Fixed token windows provide predictable sizes, while structural boundaries can preserve headings, lists and exceptions. Neither guarantees a self-contained answer.

Evaluate whether relevant facts, exclusions and provenance survive retrieval and final context assembly. Overlap increases storage and repeated context, and duplicated text can crowd out distinct evidence. Record the chunker version and parent relationship so changes can be reindexed and evaluated consistently.
Why: A positive eligibility paragraph and its immediately following exclusion must be recoverable together. A small window may separate them; a huge window may waste budget and bury the decisive clause among unrelated sections.
Risk: Tuning only average chunk length can miss answer-critical boundaries.
Trade: Combine size bounds with document structure and measured downstream evidence support.
Try: Compare two chunking policies on a rule, exclusion, table and cross-page reference.
